title: Approve, reject or defer: justifying the decision
blurb: Justify a recommendation to approve, reject or defer a change against the business case and objectives, and know who should decide.
question: Millbrook's sponsor must decide three change requests this week: a lift shaft for platform 2, a decorative glass canopy, and new digital passenger screens. How should each recommendation be justified, and what makes approve, reject or defer the right call?

teach.h: Justify it against the business case
teach.body: A change recommendation is justified by testing the evaluated change against the business case and the project objectives: do its benefits outweigh its costs and risks, and does it still serve what the project is for? In plain English: the question is never 'who wants it?' or 'how quick is it?' but 'does this make the project more worthwhile, and can we afford it?' The project manager recommends; the appropriate authority decides.

root.label: Evaluated change
root.sub: Tested against business case and objectives

children.label: Not justified
children.sub: No benefit, unaffordable, out of scope, too risky

teach.caption: Every decision is recorded with its reasons and communicated to the requester.

rows.label: Justified when
values: No benefit, too costly or risky

teach.caption: Out of scope is a reason to reject: if it does not serve this project's objectives, it may belong in another project.

head: The change is…
Decided by
teach.caption: Governance sets the limits (tolerances). The point is that decisions are made at the right level.

teach.body: CR-031 (lift): the PM recommends the partial option, building the lift shaft now, because it secures most of the accessibility benefit for far less cost and delay, and fitting the lift itself waits for confirmed funding. CR-034 (glass canopy over the car park): reject, as it adds cost with no benefit to the objectives. CR-036 (digital screens): defer, because the operator's new screen standard is not yet published, so the information needed to specify them is missing.

Decision
Justification
teach.caption: Each justification refers back to the business case, the objectives or the information available.

teach.h: A thinking aid: benefit vs urgency
teach.caption: Not an APM rule. Affordability, risk, missing information and the decision-maker's authority still apply.

teach.body: Approving too readily lets scope creep in and erodes the business case. Rejecting everything to protect the plan throws away changes that would improve the outcome. Deferring is not a polite rejection: it needs a reason and a review date or trigger, or uncertainty drags on and the cost of a later change may rise. Whatever the decision, giving the reasons keeps stakeholders' trust and leaves an audit trail.

teach.text: Classic distractors: 'approve because a senior stakeholder wants it' (seniority is not a justification), 'approve because it is quick or cheap' (without benefit it is not justified), 'reject everything to keep the plan stable' (change control enables good change), and 'the PM decides every change' (only within delegated limits; beyond them the sponsor or change authority decides).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State the test: is the change justified against the business case and objectives?
Approve: benefits outweigh costs and risks, aligned to objectives, within authority.
Reject: no benefit, unaffordable, out of scope or too risky.
Defer: not urgent, more information needed, or better in a later phase or release.
Record the decision and reasons, and tell the requester and those affected.
Recommendations are justified against the business case and project objectives.
Approve when benefits outweigh costs and risks and it is within authority.
Reject when there is no benefit, it is unaffordable, out of scope or too risky.
Defer when it is not urgent, needs more information or fits a later phase, with a review point.
The PM recommends; the appropriate authority decides; reasons are recorded and shared.

summary: You can now justify a recommendation to approve, reject or defer a change by testing it against the business case and objectives. You can also explain who should make the decision and why recording and sharing the reasons matters.

A.q: Which is the best justification for approving a change request?
options: Its benefits outweigh its costs and risks
A senior manager has asked for it to be done
The team can build it quickly and easily
It was raised before the end of the phase
A.why: A change is justified when, tested against the business case, its benefits outweigh its costs and risks and it supports the objectives.

whyNot.1: Seniority is not a justification; the business case is.
whyNot.2: Speed and ease do not make a change worthwhile if it adds no benefit.
whyNot.3: Timing of the request does not justify it.

A.q: An evaluated change would add real value, but it is not urgent and would fit more naturally into the next release. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Approve
Reject
Defer
Escalate
A.why: Not urgent and better suited to a later release are classic reasons to defer, with a review point set.

whyNot.0: Approving now would disrupt the current release for a change that can wait.
whyNot.1: It adds real value, so rejecting it would throw away a worthwhile change.
whyNot.3: Escalation is about who decides, not one of the three decisions.

A.q: Which of these is a valid reason to REJECT a change?
options: It needs more information first
It falls outside the objectives
It suits a later release better
Its benefits outweigh its costs
A.why: A change that is out of scope, offering nothing towards the project's objectives, should be rejected (it may belong elsewhere).

whyNot.0: Needing more information is a reason to defer.
whyNot.2: Better in a later release is a reason to defer.
whyNot.3: Benefits outweighing costs is a reason to approve.

B.q: An online retailer's proposed change would add £200k to the project for a feature with no measurable benefit. The board asks for a recommendation. Which is best?
options: Approve: the budget can absorb it
Reject: no benefit justifies it
Defer: wait for a later release
Approve: the board asked to see it
B.why: With no benefit, the cost cannot be justified against the business case, so the change should be rejected with the reason recorded.

whyNot.0: Being affordable does not make a change worthwhile.
whyNot.2: Deferring a change with no benefit just postpones a rejection.
whyNot.3: Asking to see a request is not a justification for approving it.

B.q: A change request is rejected. Why should the reasons be recorded and given to the person who raised it?
options: So the request can be approved later
So the requester can overrule it
So the baseline can be updated
To keep trust and an audit trail
B.why: Explaining the reasons keeps stakeholders' trust and confidence in the process, and the record shows the decision was made properly.

whyNot.0: Recording reasons does not reopen the decision.
whyNot.1: Requesters cannot overrule the appropriate authority.
whyNot.2: A rejected change does not alter the baseline.

B.q: Against what should a change recommendation mainly be justified?
options: Business case and objectives
Requester's level of seniority
Speed of putting it in place
The PM's personal preference
B.why: Recommendations are justified by testing the change against the business case and project objectives.

whyNot.1: Seniority does not make a change worthwhile.
whyNot.2: A fast change can still be a poor one.
whyNot.3: Decisions must be objective, not personal.

C.q: The detailed evaluation of a change is incomplete because a supplier's quote has not arrived, but the decision meeting is today. The change is not urgent. What is the best recommendation?
options: Approve now and confirm the cost later
Reject it, as the evaluation is incomplete
Defer it until the supplier quote arrives
Implement a trial version to test the cost
C.why: Not urgent and needing more information are both reasons to defer, with the quote as the trigger to revisit.

whyNot.0: Approving without knowing the cost risks an unaffordable change.
whyNot.1: The change may be worthwhile; missing information is a reason to wait, not to reject.
whyNot.3: Nothing should be implemented before a decision.

C.q: Millbrook's PM can approve changes up to £10k (illustrative). CR-031's shaft option costs about £120k and has strong benefits. What should the PM do?
options: Approve it, as the benefits are strong
Reject it, as it is beyond their limit
Defer it until the cost drops below £10k
Recommend approval to the sponsor
C.why: The change is beyond the PM's delegated limit, so the PM recommends approval and the sponsor or change authority decides.

whyNot.0: Strong benefits do not give the PM authority beyond their limits.
whyNot.1: Being beyond the PM's limit is a reason to escalate the decision, not to reject.
whyNot.2: Waiting for an unlikely cost fall is not a justified deferral.

C.q: Which TWO are valid reasons to DEFER a change? 1. It is not urgent 2. More information is needed 3. Its benefits clearly outweigh its costs 4. It is unaffordable at any point
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: Not urgent (1) and needing more information (2) are reasons to defer.

whyNot.0: Benefits clearly outweighing costs (3) is a reason to approve.
whyNot.2: Being unaffordable at any point (4) is a reason to reject.
whyNot.3: 3 points to approve and 4 points to reject; neither is a reason to defer.

reteach.title: Think of a family holiday budget
reteach.question: You have a fixed holiday budget and a purpose: a relaxing week for the whole family. Three requests come in: a hot-air balloon ride, a bigger hire car, and a theatre trip on a date not yet announced. How do you decide each?

blocks.body: The bigger car means everyone fits comfortably: real benefit for a small extra cost, so yes (approve). The balloon ride costs half the budget and only one person wants it: no (reject). The theatre trip sounds lovely, but the dates aren't out yet: not yet (defer), and you agree to look again when the dates are announced. Each answer is judged against the purpose and the budget, not against who asked loudest.

blocks.text: 'Not yet' only works if you actually look again. A deferral needs a review date or trigger, here the dates being announced.

explain.body: Approve when the change's benefits outweigh its costs and risks, it is aligned to the objectives, and the decision is within the decision-maker's authority. The PM can approve only within delegated limits; beyond them the sponsor or change authority decides.

test.q: When can a project manager approve a change themselves?
options: When it is within their delegated limits
Whenever the benefits look strong to them
When the sponsor is too busy to decide it
When the requester is a senior manager
test.why: Governance delegates limits (tolerances) to the PM; changes within them can be approved by the PM and recorded.

whyNot.1: Strong benefits do not extend the PM's authority.
whyNot.2: A busy sponsor does not transfer their authority to the PM.
whyNot.3: The requester's seniority does not change who has authority.

explain.body: Reject when the change brings no benefit, is unaffordable, is out of scope for this project's objectives, or is too risky for what it offers. Record the reasons and tell the requester.

test.q: Which change should most likely be rejected?
options: One that needs more information first
One that fits a later release better
One within the PM's delegated limits
One too risky for its small benefit
test.why: A change whose risk is out of proportion to its benefit is not justified, so it should be rejected.

whyNot.0: Needing more information points to deferral.
whyNot.1: Better in a later release points to deferral.
whyNot.2: Being within limits says who decides, not what the decision should be.

explain.body: Defer when the change is not urgent, more information is needed, or it fits better in a later phase or release. A deferral needs a reason and a review date or trigger; otherwise it becomes a hidden rejection or a lingering uncertainty.

test.q: What should accompany a decision to defer a change?
options: An update to the project baseline
Immediate work on a trial version
A reason and a review trigger
A new requester to take ownership
test.why: A deferral needs a recorded reason and a point at which it will be looked at again.

whyNot.0: The baseline is updated only for approved changes.
whyNot.1: No work starts on a deferred change.
whyNot.3: The original requester stays the same; ownership is not the issue.

explain.body: Approve too readily and scope creeps while the business case erodes. Reject everything and beneficial changes are lost. Defer without a trigger and uncertainty lingers. Change control is there to enable the right changes, not to block all of them.

test.q: A team decides to reject every change request to keep its plan stable. What is the main weakness of this?
options: It makes the change log harder to maintain
Changes that would help are lost
It gives the sponsor too much authority
It means the baseline must be updated
test.why: Change control exists to enable worthwhile change. Rejecting everything throws away changes that would improve the outcome or protect the benefits.

whyNot.0: The log is just as easy to keep; the problem is lost value.
whyNot.2: Rejecting everything removes decisions from the sponsor, rather than adding authority.
whyNot.3: Rejected changes do not alter the baseline.
